# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Partner], Deal Team, Ratel Dairy Holdings, LLC matter
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 7, 2026
**Re:** Ratel / Brilal: Buyer-side issues in the Sunfold Creamery Stock Purchase Agreement and Ancillary Agreements
**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed the five documents in the folder:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement dated March 16, 2026 (the **SPA**);
- the Transition Services Agreement (the **TSA**);
- the Brilal board consent dated March 16, 2026;
- the Bill of Sale for the Lagoon Assets;
- the superseded February 20, 2026 draft of SPA Article IX (the **Feb Draft**).

Ratel is buying all of the shares of Sunfold Creamery, Inc. from Brilal Foods Group, Inc. for **$86,500,000** (SPA §2.1). The general indemnity **Cap is 10% of the Purchase Price**, or **$8,650,000** (SPA §9.5(a)). The Deductible is 0.75%, or $648,750. New York law governs (SPA §12.10).

I found five issues that need to be raised with Brilal. They are listed below in order of significance to Ratel.

| # | Issue | Location | Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The Bill of Sale pulls the Specified Environmental Matter back under the 10% Cap | Bill of Sale §4.1; SPA §§9.5(b), 12.8 | The largest known environmental liability is capped at $8.65M |
| 2 | Buyer gives an uncapped, perpetual indemnity for Seller's guaranties, including pre-Closing exposure | SPA §9.3(b) | Unlimited liability on the plant lease and supply-contract guaranties |
| 3 | The Kettle Ridge change-of-control consent is not scheduled, not a closing condition, and is deferred until after Closing | Board Consent Recital 1.6 and Resolution 4; SPA §§4.3, 4.5, 7.2(d), Sch. 4.5 | Kettle Ridge (about 40% of raw milk) can terminate on 30 days' notice; a rep claim faces a *Galli v. Metz* defense |
| 4 | The TSA confidentiality definition is narrow and exclusive, and overrides SPA §6.7 | TSA §§7.1, 7.3, 7.6; SPA §§1.1, 6.7, 12.8 | Unmarked supplier pricing and customer data lose protection for the 12-month Service Period |
| 5 | Seller may assign the TSA freely, including to a competitor | TSA §12.3; SPA §12.4 | A competitor could take over testing, certification and logistics and receive Company data |

A recurring theme drives Issues 1 and 4. **SPA §12.8** provides that, in any conflict, "the Ancillary Agreement shall control as to its subject matter." Brilal has used the Ancillary Agreements to override negotiated SPA protections. Fixing the individual provisions is necessary. We should also revise §12.8 itself (proposed language in Part III).

**Assumptions.**

- **Closing status.** Several documents are dated April 30, 2026, which is the scheduled Closing Date. The SPA outside date in §8.1(b) is June 30, 2026. Because you asked what Ratel needs "to close," I assume Closing has **not** occurred, the TSA and Bill of Sale remain Exhibit forms open to negotiation, and the outside date has been or will be extended in writing. If Closing has already occurred, each fix below becomes a post-Closing amendment. That requires a written instrument signed by both Parties (SPA §12.3; TSA §12.2; Bill of Sale §6.2), and Ratel's negotiating leverage is much reduced. **Please confirm the status.**
- **Kettle Ridge contract.** I have not seen the Raw Milk Supply Agreement. I rely on the board consent's description of it.
- **Feb Draft.** I treat the Feb Draft as superseded. It has no operative effect. It is useful only as evidence of the previously negotiated position.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: The Bill of Sale brings the Specified Environmental Matter back under the 10% Cap

**Location.**
- Bill of Sale §4.1 (Claims – Recovery)
- SPA §1.1 ("Specified Environmental Matter," "Lagoon Assets," "Ancillary Agreements")
- SPA §§9.2(c), 9.5(b)(iii) and 12.8

**What the documents say.**

- **SPA definitions and carve-out.** The SPA defines the Specified Environmental Matter as "contamination originating from the St. Albans Plant wastewater lagoon system." Seller indemnifies for it under §9.2(c), and claims may be brought for seven years (§9.1). Section 9.5(b)(iii) expressly provides that the Deductible and the Cap "shall not apply" to Losses from the Specified Environmental Matter, "whether claimed under Section 9.2(a) or Section 9.2(c)."
- **Bill of Sale §4.1.** The Bill of Sale conveys the Lagoon Assets, meaning the very lagoon system that is the source of the Specified Environmental Matter. Section 4.1 then provides: "All Losses arising out of or relating to the Conveyed Assets or the underlying real property … **including any Environmental Liability**, shall be recoverable … solely under … Article IX of the Purchase Agreement, and **subject to the Cap**."
- **Order of precedence.** The Bill of Sale is an "Ancillary Agreement" under SPA §1.1. SPA §12.8 says the Ancillary Agreement "shall control as to its subject matter." The subject matter of the Bill of Sale is the Lagoon Assets and claims relating to them.

**Why it matters to Ratel.**

- **The carve-out is effectively undone.** Lagoon contamination plainly "arise[s] out of or relat[es] to the Conveyed Assets," and the Bill of Sale controls as to that subject matter. Seller will argue that its total liability for the Specified Environmental Matter is capped at **$8,650,000**. The SPA §9.5(b)(iii) carve-out was the central protection for the best-known environmental risk in the deal. Seller has disclosed it as an exception to the §4.8 environmental rep, and Seller controls the remediation under §9.4(c).
- **The cap may reach beyond the SPA's own cap.** SPA §9.5(a) caps only §9.2(a) rep claims. The Bill of Sale applies "the Cap" to *all* Losses relating to the lagoon assets "and the underlying real property." Seller can argue this caps the stand-alone §9.2(c) indemnity, which has no cap of any kind under the SPA. It could also cap non-environmental claims, including breach of the §3.1 title warranty.
- **The capped claims draw down the general pool.** Lagoon remediation costs counted against the Cap would also consume capacity needed for ordinary rep-breach claims.
- **Remediation costs can run high.** Investigation, closure and groundwater monitoring for a dairy wastewater lagoon, together with ANR penalties and third-party claims, can readily exceed $8.65M. Ratel would bear the excess through its ownership of the Company, which will own the lagoon after Closing.

Seller may respond that §9.5(b) prevails as the more specific provision. Ratel should not rely on that argument. Section 12.8 is an express precedence rule, and New York courts enforce such clauses as written.

**Recommendation.**

**(a) Amend Bill of Sale §4.1.**

> "4.1 Recovery. All Losses arising out of or relating to the Conveyed Assets or the underlying real property on which the Conveyed Assets are located, including any Environmental Liability, shall be recoverable by the Company, Buyer and the other Buyer Indemnitees under, and in accordance with the procedures of, Article IX of the Purchase Agreement, **subject only to those limitations in Article IX of the Purchase Agreement that would apply to the relevant claim if made directly under the Purchase Agreement. For the avoidance of doubt, nothing in this Bill of Sale shall (a) subject any Losses arising out of or relating to the Specified Environmental Matter, or any claim under Section 9.2(c) of the Purchase Agreement, to the Deductible or the Cap, or (b) shorten any survival period under Section 9.1 of the Purchase Agreement.** Losses under Section 3.1 or 3.2 of this Bill of Sale shall be treated as Losses arising out of a breach of a Fundamental Representation."

**(b) Revise SPA §12.8** so that the SPA's indemnification provisions always prevail (see Part III).

**(c) Add an express statement** to SPA §9.5(b) that the carve-out applies "notwithstanding any provision of any Ancillary Agreement."

---

### Issue 2: Buyer's uncapped, perpetual indemnity for the Company Guaranties

**Location.**
- SPA §9.3(b)
- SPA §9.5(a) (last sentence)
- SPA §1.1 ("Company Guaranties") and Schedule 1.1(a)
- SPA §6.6
- Feb Draft §§9.3(b) and 9.5(a)(iii), for comparison

**What the documents say.**

- **The indemnity.** Section 9.3(b) requires Buyer to indemnify the Seller Indemnitees for "all Losses … arising out of or relating to … the Company Guaranties, including any payment, performance or other obligation of Seller … under any Company Guaranty, **whether arising before or after the Closing**, and **notwithstanding Section 9.5**."
- **What is guaranteed.** Under Schedule 1.1(a), the Company Guaranties are Brilal's guaranties of the St. Albans Plant lease and of the Company's packaging and ingredient supply contracts.
- **The guaranties survive Closing.** Section 6.6 expressly carves the Company Guaranties out of the intercompany terminations. They therefore stay in place after Closing.
- **The cap protects only Buyer's other indemnity.** The Buyer cap in §9.5(a) ("Buyer shall not be liable under Section 9.3(a) for Losses in excess of the Cap") covers only §9.3(a).

**Why it matters to Ratel.**

- **No limits apply.** The phrase "notwithstanding Section 9.5" removes every limitation in §9.5: the Cap, the Deductible, the insurance-offset rule and the punitive-damages exclusion.
- **No time limit applies.** Section 9.1 sets survival periods for *representations*. A §9.3(b) indemnity is a covenant-type obligation with no stated end date. Ratel's exposure therefore lasts for the full remaining term of the plant lease and the supply contracts, plus any renewals.
- **Ratel pays for Seller's pre-Closing liabilities.** "Whether arising before … the Closing" makes Ratel responsible for guaranty calls relating to pre-Closing defaults by the Company. Those liabilities arose while Brilal owned and controlled the Company, and they are Seller's economic responsibility. This also sits uneasily with §9.2, under which Seller bears pre-Closing liabilities, and the two provisions could produce circular claims.
- **Ratel has no path to end the exposure.** Seller has no obligation to seek releases of the guaranties. Buyer has no right to replace them.
- **The term departed from the earlier deal.** In the Feb Draft, §9.3(b) covered only obligations that "first arise[] and [are] attributable to the period after the Closing," and §9.5(a)(iii) capped *all* of §9.3. The current language departs from that earlier negotiated position. We should ask Brilal to explain the change, and we can use the Feb Draft as leverage.

**Recommendation.** Restore the Feb Draft scope, cap the indemnity, and add a release covenant and a sunset.

**(a) Replace SPA §9.3(b):**

> "(b) any payment or performance by Seller or any of its Affiliates under a Company Guaranty after the Closing, solely to the extent that payment or performance relates to an obligation of the Company that first arises after, and is attributable to the period after, the Closing, and excluding any obligation arising out of any breach, default or event occurring at or before the Closing."

**(b) Amend the last sentence of §9.5(a):**

> "Buyer shall not be liable under Section 9.3 for Losses in excess of the Cap."

**(c) Add a new SPA §6.12:**

> "6.12 Company Guaranties. Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain, at or before the Closing, the full and unconditional release of Seller and its Affiliates from each Company Guaranty. To the extent any Company Guaranty is not released at the Closing, Buyer shall use commercially reasonable efforts (which shall not require the payment of any consideration or the provision of any credit support exceeding that provided by Seller as of the date of this Agreement) to obtain that release within 180 days after the Closing Date. Seller shall not amend, extend or renew any Company Guaranty without Buyer's prior written consent. Buyer's obligations under Section 9.3(b) shall terminate with respect to each Company Guaranty on the earlier of its release and the expiration of the current term of the underlying Contract, without renewal."

**(d) Fallback.** If Brilal insists on keeping the indemnity uncapped, at a minimum strike "whether arising before or after the Closing" and limit the indemnity to post-Closing obligations, so that pre-Closing exposure remains with Seller under §9.2.

---

### Issue 3: The Kettle Ridge change-of-control consent is unaddressed and deferred until after Closing

**Location.**
- Brilal Board Consent, Recital 1.6 and Resolution 4
- SPA §§4.3(c), 4.5 and 4.6(a)
- SPA §§6.3, 7.2(d) and 3.2(a)(vi)
- SPA Schedule 4.5

**What the documents say.**

- **The board consent's disclosure.** Recital 1.6 records the following:
  - Kettle Ridge Organic Dairy Cooperative supplies about **40%** of the Company's raw milk under the Raw Milk Supply Agreement.
  - A "change in control of the Company requires the prior written consent of Kettle Ridge, failing which Kettle Ridge may terminate … on 30 days' notice."
  - The sale to Ratel "will constitute a change in control."
- **Resolution 4.** Officers are "authorized to request such consent **following the Closing**."
- **The SPA reps.**
  - SPA §4.5 represents that no third-party consents are required "except as set forth on Schedule 4.5."
  - SPA §4.3(c) gives a similar no-conflicts rep, also keyed to Schedule 4.5.
  - Schedule 4.5 lists only the landlord consent, the notice to the organic certifier and the notice to the Vermont ANR. **Kettle Ridge is not on it.** Recital 1.5 of the board consent mirrors this omission.
- **Closing mechanics.** Section 7.2(d) conditions Closing only on the Schedule 4.5 consents. Seller's efforts covenant in §6.3 and the delivery obligation in §3.2(a)(vi) are likewise limited to Schedule 4.5. **The Kettle Ridge consent is therefore not a condition to Closing.** Seller has no obligation to obtain it before Closing, and its own board has decided not to.

**Why it matters to Ratel.**

- **Supply risk.** Losing 40% of raw milk supply on 30 days' notice would be a serious operational blow to an organic processor. Certified organic raw milk cannot be quickly replaced from the spot market without risk to supply and to organic certification. The Kettle Ridge contract is also a Material Contract under §4.6(a). Termination, or a consent extracted at a higher price, would directly erode deal value.
- **Leverage shifts to Kettle Ridge.** Requesting consent only after Closing gives Kettle Ridge maximum leverage to renegotiate pricing or terms, and Ratel bears that cost.
- **A rep claim is weak.**
  - **The disclosure defense.** Sections 4.3 and 4.5 appear inaccurate, so a rep-breach claim under §9.2(a) is available in theory. The claim is weak, however. Under New York law (*Galli v. Metz*, 973 F.2d 145 (2d Cir. 1992), distinguishing *CBS Inc. v. Ziff-Davis Publishing Co.*, 75 N.Y.2d 496 (1990)), a buyer that closes knowing, *from the seller's own disclosure*, that a warranty is untrue may be held to have waived the breach unless it expressly preserves its rights.
  - **Ratel's likely knowledge.** The board consent will be certified and delivered to Ratel at Closing under §3.2(a)(vii). The disclosure is therefore in Ratel's hands.
  - **No contractual protection.** The SPA has no pro-sandbagging clause. Section 5.5 recites reliance on Ratel's own investigation.
  - **Limits even if the claim succeeds.** Any recovery would be subject to the Deductible and the $8.65M Cap.

**Recommendation.** The preferred fix is to make the consent a closing condition. If Brilal resists, Ratel should insist on a specific, uncapped indemnity and a reservation of rights.

**(a) Add to Schedule 4.5:**

> "4. Consent of Kettle Ridge Organic Dairy Cooperative under the Raw Milk Supply Agreement to the change of control of the Company, without amendment of the pricing, volume, term or other material terms of the Raw Milk Supply Agreement."

Adding this item automatically brings the consent within §§6.3, 7.2(d) and 3.2(a)(vi).

**(b) If Brilal will not accept a closing condition, add a new §9.2(e) and a carve-out in §9.5(b):**

> "(e) any termination, non-renewal or adverse modification of the Raw Milk Supply Agreement with Kettle Ridge Organic Dairy Cooperative, or any failure to obtain the consent of Kettle Ridge to the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, in each case occurring within 24 months after the Closing Date, including the incremental cost of replacement certified organic raw milk for the remainder of the then-current term."

Add "(iv) Section 9.2(e)" to the Deductible and Cap exclusions in §9.5(b). Consider a separate limit or an escrow sized to the cost of replacement supply.

**(c) Add a reservation of rights / pro-sandbagging clause** (new §9.8):

> "The rights of the Buyer Indemnitees to indemnification shall not be affected or limited by any investigation by or knowledge of Buyer or its representatives, whether acquired before or after the date of this Agreement or the Closing Date, including any knowledge obtained from Seller or any document delivered by Seller, and Buyer's consummation of the Closing shall not constitute a waiver of any such right."

**(d) If closing on the current documents is unavoidable**, deliver a written reservation-of-rights letter at or before Closing that specifically identifies the §§4.3 and 4.5 inaccuracy relating to Kettle Ridge.

**(e) Diligence.** Ratel should obtain and review the Raw Milk Supply Agreement itself to confirm the following points, which I have not been able to verify:
- the exact consent mechanics;
- whether an equity sale, as opposed to an assignment, triggers the clause;
- the term and renewal provisions.

SPA §6.8(b) prohibits Seller from soliciting Company milk suppliers. It does not protect Ratel against Kettle Ridge acting on its own.

---

### Issue 4: The TSA's narrow and exclusive "Confidential Information" definition strips SPA protection from Company data

**Location.**
- TSA §§7.1, 7.3, 7.5, 7.6 and 6.2
- SPA §1.1 ("Company Confidential Information")
- SPA §§6.7 and 12.8

**What the documents say.**

- **The SPA standard.** SPA §6.7 requires Seller to hold "Company Confidential Information" in strict confidence. SPA §1.1 defines that term broadly: all non-public Company information "whether or not marked or identified as confidential," including customer lists and order data, farm supplier identities and pricing, herd records, product formulas, organic certification files and laboratory testing data. Section 6.7 confirms that unmarked information is covered.
- **The TSA definition.** TSA §7.1 defines "Confidential Information" as information disclosed "in written, electronic or other tangible form, that is **marked as confidential at the time of disclosure**."
- **Exclusivity.** TSA §7.3 provides that Provider's obligations for Company information received in performing the Services "are **governed exclusively by this Section 7**."
- **Precedence.** SPA §12.8 lets the TSA control as to its subject matter.

**Why it matters to Ratel.**

- **The Company must hand over its most sensitive data.** Under TSA §6.2, the Company is *required* to give Brilal raw milk samples, supplier organic certificates, production schedules and **customer order data**. Brilal will also generate test results and organic system plan files. That flow continues for the 12-month Service Period, plus any extension under §3.2.
- **Most of that data will be unprotected.** It will routinely move through operational channels without confidentiality markings, and some of it will be oral. Because §7.3 is exclusive and the TSA controls under §12.8, Brilal can argue that SPA §6.7 does not apply to any information received through the TSA. On that reading, unmarked supplier pricing, customer orders and lab data are unprotected.
- **Exception (b) could swallow the rule.** TSA §7.1(b) excludes information "known to the Receiving Party without restriction before disclosure." As the Company's former parent, Brilal knew essentially all Company information before Closing. Brilal could invoke this exception to exclude almost everything.
- **The protection is also too short.** TSA §7.6 limits the obligations to three years after the Service Period. SPA §6.7 has no end date. The backup-retention exception in §7.5 adds further leakage.
- **The competitive risk is real.** Brilal remains in the food business, and Seller's non-compete under SPA §6.8 lasts only three years. Customer and supplier pricing in Brilal's hands is a genuine competitive threat.

**Recommendation.**

**(a) Replace TSA §7.3:**

> "7.3 Company Information. All information of or concerning the Company received by Provider, its Affiliates or Provider Personnel in connection with this Agreement or the performance of the Services, in any form and whether or not marked or identified as confidential, constitutes Company Confidential Information (as defined in the Purchase Agreement) and is subject to Section 6.7 of the Purchase Agreement in addition to this Section 7. The exclusions in clauses (b) and (d) of Section 7.1 shall not apply to Company Confidential Information. In the event of any conflict between this Section 7 and Section 6.7 of the Purchase Agreement, the provision more protective of the Company shall control, notwithstanding Section 12.8 of the Purchase Agreement."

**(b) Delete the words** "in written, electronic or other tangible form, that is marked as confidential at the time of disclosure" from §7.1, at least as applied to information disclosed by the Company.

**(c) Amend §7.6** so that obligations relating to Company Confidential Information continue for as long as SPA §6.7 applies.

**(d) Require Provider** to certify return or destruction, and limit the backup exception to systems not accessible in the ordinary course.

---

### Issue 5: Seller may assign the TSA freely, including to a competitor

**Location.**
- TSA §§12.3 and 2.4
- SPA §12.4

**What the documents say.**

- **The incorporation.** TSA §12.3 provides that assignment "is governed by Section 12.4 of the Purchase Agreement, **mutatis mutandis**, with Provider in the position of Seller and the Company in the position of Buyer."
- **The incorporated clause.** SPA §12.4 provides that Buyer may not assign without Seller's consent, and that "Seller may assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations under it **without the consent of Buyer**."
- **The result.** Read together, Brilal may assign the TSA to anyone without the Company's consent. The Company cannot assign without Brilal's consent.

**Why it matters to Ratel.**

- **A competitor could take over core services.** Brilal could assign the TSA to a competing organic dairy processor or its affiliate. That assignee would then:
  - run the Company's raw milk and finished-product testing;
  - maintain its organic system plan;
  - handle its cold-chain logistics;
  - receive production schedules and customer order data under §6.2.
- **The non-compete would not reach the assignee.** SPA §6.8 binds only Seller and its Affiliates. An unaffiliated assignee would be outside it.
- **The TSA confidentiality terms are weak.** Those terms have the gaps described in Issue 4.
- **Ratel has no meaningful remedy.**
  - The Company has no consent right.
  - It has no termination right tied to assignment.
  - Nothing confirms that Brilal remains liable after an assignment. The §2.4 subcontractor-responsibility language does not address assignees.
  - The Company could terminate individual Services for convenience on 30 days' notice under §9.1. In practice, that is not a substitute while the Company depends on the Services during the transition.
- **The SPA itself has the same problem.** SPA §12.4 lets Seller assign "any of its rights *or obligations*" under the SPA without consent. That includes its Article IX indemnity obligations, among them the seven-year Specified Environmental Matter indemnity. Brilal could shift those obligations to a thinly capitalized affiliate or third party.

**Recommendation.**

**(a) Replace TSA §12.3:**

> "12.3 Assignment. Neither Party may assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations under it, by operation of law, change of control or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other Party, which shall not be unreasonably withheld, except that the Company may assign this Agreement, without consent, to Buyer, any Affiliate of Buyer, any lender as collateral, or any acquirer of all or substantially all of the Company's business. Without limiting the foregoing, it shall be reasonable for the Company to withhold consent to any assignment to, or any change of control of Provider in favor of, any Person (or Affiliate of a Person) engaged in the processing or sale of dairy products. No permitted assignment by Provider shall relieve Provider of its obligations under this Agreement. If Provider assigns or purports to assign this Agreement, or any Service is performed by a Person engaged in the processing or sale of dairy products, the Company may terminate this Agreement or any Service immediately on written notice without liability, and Provider shall provide the migration assistance described in Section 6.4 at no additional charge. Any purported assignment in violation of this Section 12.3 is void."

**(b) Revise SPA §12.4** so that it is mutual. Permit Buyer to assign to Affiliates, lenders and successors without consent. Add:

> "No assignment by Seller shall relieve Seller of any of its obligations under this Agreement, including under Article IX."

---

## III. Cross-Cutting Fix: SPA §12.8 (Order of Precedence)

Issues 1 and 4 both depend on the "Ancillary Agreement controls as to its subject matter" rule. I recommend replacing §12.8:

> "12.8 Ancillary Agreements. In the event of any conflict or inconsistency between this Agreement and any Ancillary Agreement, this Agreement shall control, except that the Transition Services Agreement shall control solely with respect to the scope, standard of performance, fees and term of the Services. Notwithstanding the foregoing or anything to the contrary in any Ancillary Agreement, (a) no Ancillary Agreement shall limit, restrict or reduce any right or remedy of any Buyer Indemnitee under Article IX, or subject any Loss to the Deductible, the Cap or any survival period to which it would not be subject under this Agreement, and (b) no Ancillary Agreement shall limit Seller's obligations under Section 6.7."

---

## IV. Other Observations

These points are lower priority and could be raised if the negotiating context allows.

1. **Feb Draft.** The Feb Draft is superseded and has no operative effect. Its §9.3(b) and §9.5(a)(iii) positions are useful precedent for Issue 2. Its §9.5(f) mitigation covenant was dropped from the signed SPA, which favors Buyer, and we should not reintroduce it.
2. **TSA liability cap.** TSA §8.1 caps Provider's liability at total Fees, excluding confidentiality breaches. A spoilage or recall event could exceed that amount, for example a lab failure that releases a contaminated lot. Section 8.2(c) indemnifies only third-party claims. Consider carving the Company's own recall and spoilage losses out of the Fee cap.
3. **Sufficiency rep.** SPA §4.7's sufficiency rep relies on the TSA Services. If Seller assigns the TSA or reduces the Services, the gap should be covered by the Issue 5 termination and migration rights.

---

## V. Recommended Next Steps

1. Confirm whether Closing has occurred and whether the June 30, 2026 outside date has been extended.
2. Send Brilal a markup covering:
   - Bill of Sale §4.1;
   - SPA §§9.3(b), 9.5(a), 9.5(b), 12.4, 12.8 and new §§6.12, 9.2(e) and 9.8;
   - Schedule 4.5;
   - TSA §§7.1, 7.3, 7.6 and 12.3.
3. Request a copy of the Kettle Ridge Raw Milk Supply Agreement. Ask Brilal to explain why the Kettle Ridge consent was left off Schedule 4.5 even though its own board recorded it.
4. Have Ratel's environmental consultant prepare a range estimate for lagoon investigation and closure costs, to quantify the Issue 1 exposure against the $8.65M Cap.

## II. Issues, in Order of Significance

- **Where it is missing in the SPA.**
  - SPA §4.5 represents that no third-party consent is required except as listed on Schedule 4.5. Schedule 4.5 lists only three items: the landlord consent, the certifying agent notice and the ANR notice. Kettle Ridge is not listed.
  - Recital 1.5 of the board consent describes the Schedule 4.5 items as the only consents the Transaction requires.
  - The §7.2(d) closing condition, the §3.2(a)(vi) deliverable and the §6.3 efforts covenant all reach only Schedule 4.5 consents.
- **Result.** Seller has no obligation to obtain the Kettle Ridge consent before Closing. Ratel has no right to refuse to close if the consent is not obtained.

**Why it matters to Ratel**
- **Supply risk.** Losing 40% of the organic raw milk supply on 30 days' notice would be a business-critical event for a creamery. Certified organic milk cannot be quickly replaced on the spot market, and Kettle Ridge gains leverage to reprice.
- **The rep remedy is weak.**
  - On its face, §4.5 is inaccurate, and the §4.3(c) no-conflicts rep is likely breached as well.
  - Any claim under §9.2(a) is subject to the $648,750 Deductible, the $8,650,000 Cap and the 18-month survival period. That may not cover the loss of a principal supplier.
  - Under New York law (*Galli v. Metz*, 973 F.2d 145 (2d Cir. 1992), and its progeny), a buyer that closes knowing, from the seller's own disclosure, that a rep is untrue may be found to have waived the breach. That applies unless the buyer expressly preserves its rights.
  - Brilal will argue it disclosed the Kettle Ridge consent requirement. Ratel has the board consent and will receive it certified under §3.2(a)(vii), and Resolution 4 expressly contemplates "cooperation with the Buyer." Brilal will say Ratel cannot have relied on §4.5.
  - The SPA contains no pro-sandbagging clause to blunt this defense.

**Recommendation**
- **First choice:** add Kettle Ridge to Schedule 4.5, making its consent a §7.2(d) condition and a §3.2(a)(vi) deliverable.
- **Fallback if Brilal will not agree:** a specific, uncapped, first-dollar indemnity for losses from any Kettle Ridge termination or adverse amendment, with a survival period running through the remaining contract term.
- **In either case:**
  - add a pro-sandbagging clause; and
  - if Ratel closes without the consent, deliver a written reservation of rights at or before Closing.

**Proposed language**

> *Schedule 4.5, new item 4:* "Consent of Kettle Ridge Organic Dairy Cooperative under the Raw Milk Supply Agreement to the change in control of the Company, including a waiver of any right to terminate or modify the Raw Milk Supply Agreement arising from the transactions contemplated by this Agreement."

> *New §9.2(e):* "any termination, non-renewal, or adverse modification of the Raw Milk Supply Agreement with Kettle Ridge Organic Dairy Cooperative by reason of the consummation of the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, including incremental costs of replacement organic raw milk for the remaining term of that agreement."

> *Add to §9.5(b):* "(iv) Losses under Section 9.2(e)."

> *New §9.8 (Reliance):* "The rights of the Buyer Indemnitees to indemnification shall not be affected or limited by any investigation conducted by or on behalf of Buyer, or by any knowledge acquired or capable of being acquired by Buyer at any time, whether before or after the execution of this Agreement or the Closing, with respect to the accuracy or inaccuracy of any representation or warranty, and Buyer's waiver of any closing condition shall not affect its right to indemnification."

### 2. Buyer's uncapped, perpetual indemnity for Seller's guaranties, including pre-Closing exposure

**Location**
- SPA §9.3(b).
- Read with §§9.1, 9.5(a) and 6.6, and Schedule 1.1(a).

**Issue**
- §9.3(b) requires Ratel to indemnify Seller for all Losses arising out of or relating to the Company Guaranties. These are Brilal's guaranties of the St. Albans Plant lease and of the Company's packaging and ingredient supply contracts.
- The indemnity applies "*whether arising before or after the Closing,* and *notwithstanding Section 9.5*."
- The §9.5(a) limits on Buyer apply only to §9.3(a). The final SPA dropped the February draft language that capped Buyer's liability under all of §9.3.
- The "notwithstanding Section 9.5" wording removes Ratel's indemnity from the Cap, the Deductible and every other §9.5 limitation, including the insurance offset.
- §9.1 sets no survival period for this covenant. It therefore runs indefinitely.
- No SPA provision requires Seller to obtain releases of the guaranties. §6.6 expressly preserves them past Closing.

**Why it matters to Ratel**
- **Unlimited amount.** Ratel's exposure has no dollar limit and is tied to the full remaining plant lease obligations.
- **Pre-Closing liabilities shift to Ratel.** Ratel would reimburse Brilal for guaranty calls based on Company defaults that occurred while Brilal owned and controlled the Company. That is Seller's economic risk and is already priced into the $86,500,000.
- **Circular recovery risk.** Brilal could make a Company default under a supply contract, caused by pre-Closing conduct, into a claim against Ratel. This would sit outside the Cap.
- **No end date.** Because Brilal is never required to obtain releases, the exposure has no natural end.
- **The February draft is a useful negotiating anchor.** It limited §9.3(b) to obligations that "first arise and [are] attributable to the period after the Closing," and capped Buyer's §9.3 liability at the Cap.

**Recommendation**
- Limit §9.3(b) to post-Closing obligations.
- Delete "notwithstanding Section 9.5" and make §9.3(b) subject to the Cap.
- Add an affirmative covenant requiring Seller to obtain guaranty releases, with a sunset on Buyer's indemnity.
- Add a reciprocal Seller indemnity for pre-Closing guaranty-related Losses.

**Proposed language**

> *Replace §9.3(b):* "(b) any payment or performance by Seller or any of its Affiliates under a Company Guaranty after the Closing, solely to the extent that payment or performance relates to an obligation of the Company that first arises and is attributable to the period after the Closing Date and does not result from any breach by Seller of this Agreement."

> *Amend §9.5(a), last sentence:* "Buyer shall not be liable under Section 9.3 for Losses in excess of the Cap."

> *New §6.12 (Guaranty Releases):* "Seller shall use reasonable best efforts to obtain, at or before the Closing and in any event within 90 days after the Closing Date, the full and unconditional release of Seller and its Affiliates from each Company Guaranty. Buyer shall reasonably cooperate, including by offering a replacement guaranty or credit support of Buyer of substantially equivalent scope. Buyer's obligations under Section 9.3(b) with respect to any Company Guaranty shall terminate on the earlier of the release of that Company Guaranty and the second anniversary of the Closing Date."

> *New §9.2(f):* "any obligation of Seller or its Affiliates under any Company Guaranty to the extent relating to any obligation of the Company arising or attributable to any period ending on or before the Closing Date."

### 3. TSA confidentiality definition is narrower than the SPA and displaces SPA §6.7 for Services data

**Location**
- TSA §§7.1, 7.3 and 7.6.
- SPA §1.1 ("Company Confidential Information"), §6.7 and §12.8.

**Issue**
- **SPA protection is broad.** SPA §6.7 obliges Seller to hold "Company Confidential Information" in strict confidence. SPA §1.1 defines that term to cover all non-public Company information, "whether or not marked or identified as confidential." It expressly includes:
  - customer lists and order data;
  - farm supplier identities and pricing;
  - herd records;
  - product formulas;
  - organic certification files; and
  - lab testing data.
- **TSA protection is narrow.** TSA §7.1 defines "Confidential Information" only as information in tangible form "*marked as confidential at the time of disclosure*."
- **The TSA is exclusive.** TSA §7.3 provides that Brilal's obligations for Company information received in performing the Services are "*governed exclusively by this Section 7*."
- **The TSA controls.** SPA §12.8 lets an Ancillary Agreement control "as to its subject matter." Brilal will therefore argue that TSA §7 displaces SPA §6.7 for anything it receives through the Services.

**Why it matters to Ratel**
- **Brilal will hold the Company's most sensitive data, mostly unmarked.** For 12 months, and up to 15 with the §3.2 extension, Brilal will perform raw milk testing, organic compliance and cold-chain logistics.
- **The Company is required to supply that data.** TSA §6.2 obliges the Company to deliver supplier organic certificates, production schedules and customer order data. In day-to-day operations, these will arrive as unmarked load tickets, emails, test feeds and routing data.
- **Unmarked data loses protection.** Under TSA §7.1 that information is not Confidential Information. Because of §7.3, it may also fall outside SPA §6.7.
- **Oral or visual information is unprotected.** Information obtained by Provider Personnel on-site at the St. Albans Plant falls outside both "tangible" and "marked."
- **The TSA obligations expire.** TSA §7.6 ends them three years after the Service Period. SPA §6.7 is perpetual.
- **The non-compete does not fill the gap.** Brilal is subject to the SPA §6.8 non-compete, but only for three years and only in seven states. Supplier pricing and customer order data are exactly what a competitor would want.

**Recommendation**
- Conform the TSA definition to the SPA.
- Reverse the exclusivity in §7.3 so the SPA protection is additive.
- Carve Company data out of the TSA duration limit.

**Proposed language**

> *Replace TSA §7.1, first sentence:* "'**Confidential Information**' means (a) with respect to the Company, all Company Confidential Information (as defined in the Purchase Agreement), in any form and whether or not marked or identified as confidential, including all information obtained by Provider or Provider Personnel through access to the St. Albans Plant or in performing the Services; and (b) with respect to Provider, any non-public business, technical or financial information disclosed by Provider to the Company in connection with this Agreement that is marked or identified as confidential."

> *Replace TSA §7.3:* "Provider's obligations under this Section 7 with respect to information of the Company are in addition to, and not in limitation of, Provider's obligations under Section 6.7 of the Purchase Agreement. In the event of any inconsistency, the provision more protective of the Company shall control, and Section 12.8 of the Purchase Agreement shall not apply to this Section 7."

> *Amend TSA §7.6:* "...except that Provider's obligations with respect to Company Confidential Information shall continue for so long as Section 6.7 of the Purchase Agreement remains in effect."

### 4. TSA assignment clause lets Brilal assign freely, including to a competitor

**Location**
- TSA §12.3, incorporating SPA §12.4 "mutatis mutandis."
- Related provisions: TSA §2.4 (subcontractors) and §9 (termination).

**Issue**
- **The incorporation.** TSA §12.3 provides that assignment is "governed by Section 12.4 of the Purchase Agreement, mutatis mutandis," with Provider in Seller's position and the Company in Buyer's.
- **What SPA §12.4 says.**
  - Buyer may not assign without Seller's consent.
  - Seller "may assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations under it without the consent of Buyer."
- **The result.**
  - Brilal may assign the TSA, or delegate any Service, to anyone without the Company's consent. That includes a competing organic dairy processor or a buyer of Brilal's Burlington lab or fleet.
  - The Company cannot assign without Brilal's consent.
- **No offsetting protection.** No change-of-provider termination right exists. The only exit is the 30-day convenience termination in §9.1, which leaves the Company without the Service.

**Why it matters to Ratel**
- **The assignee would sit in the middle of the Company's operations.** It would test every incoming raw milk load, maintain the organic system plan and run customer deliveries.
- **The assignee would see core competitive data.** It would see the supplier, customer and pricing data discussed in Item 3. An assignee would argue it is not bound by SPA §6.7 or §6.8.
- **The non-compete could be circumvented.** Free assignment could undercut the protections Ratel paid for in the SPA.
- **Ratel's own flexibility is restricted.** The asymmetry also limits Ratel's financing and post-Closing restructuring options. For example, Ratel might need to assign the TSA to an acquisition-financing lender or to an affiliate.

**Recommendation**
- Replace the incorporation by reference with a stand-alone, mutual consent requirement.
- Permit the Company to assign to affiliates, lenders and successors.
- Give the Company a termination right, with transition assistance, on any assignment or change of control of Provider.
- Bar delegation of Services to competitors.

**Proposed language**

> *Replace TSA §12.3:* "Neither Party may assign this Agreement or any of its rights or delegate any of its obligations under it without the prior written consent of the other Party, and any purported assignment without that consent shall be void; *provided* that the Company may, without Provider's consent, assign this Agreement (a) to Buyer or any Affiliate of Buyer, (b) collaterally to any lender or agent providing financing to Buyer or the Company, or (c) to any successor to all or substantially all of the business of the Company. In no event shall Provider assign this Agreement, or delegate or subcontract any Service, to any Person that is, or is an Affiliate of, a Competitor. '**Competitor**' means any Person engaged in processing or selling organic fluid milk, yogurt or cheese. If Provider undergoes a change of control or purports to assign this Agreement, the Company may terminate this Agreement or any Service immediately on written notice without penalty, and Section 6.4 shall apply from the date of that notice."

> *Conforming change to TSA §2.4:* "...provided that Provider shall not use any subcontractor that is a Competitor, and shall obtain the Company's prior written consent (not to be unreasonably withheld) before subcontracting all or substantially all of any Service."
